messages.subject: Re: [geomorph-r-package] Odd R2 using procD.pgls
messages.body_plain:
Hi Mike,

I didn't get back to you about this - but might be useful for others. The issue was caused by some very short edges on my tree (Dean pointed out it could be a tree issue before). I seem to have solved it by rescaling the edge lengths using the chronos function in ape.

Cheers,
Charles

On Saturday, September 22, 2018 at 8:13:35 PM UTC+1, Michael Collyer wrote:

> Charles,
>
> Is it possible that with your function to obtain mean shapes by species names (tip.labels), in one case (GLS) you accidentally used raw landmark coordinates for the x argument in your function?  Such a huge effect - association of CS and shape - suggests that the coordinates were not adjusted to be the same size via GPA.  This would be especially true if one specimen (at least) was large compared to some others.  Below is an example for how such a thing could manifest, and see how it looks similar to your example.
>
> Cheers!
> Mike
>

> > data("plethspecies")
> > plethspecies$land[,,1] <- plethspecies$land[,,1] * 10 # make one really large specimen
> > Y.gpa <- gpagen(plethspecies$land)
>   |======================================================| 100%
> > gdf <- geomorph.data.frame(land = plethspecies$land, Csize = Y.gpa$Csize)
> > fit <- procD.pgls(land ~ Csize, phy = plethspecies$phy, data = gdf)
>
> Sums of Squares calculations: 1000 permutations.
>   |=====================================================================| 100%
> > summary(fit)
>
> Call:
> procD.pgls(f1 = land ~ Csize, phy = plethspecies$phy, data = gdf)
>
> Type I (Sequential) Sums of Squares and Cross-products
> Randomized Residual Permutation Procedure Used
> 1000 Permutations
> ANOVA effect sizes and P-values based on empirical F distributions
>
>
>           Df     SS     MS     Rsq      F      Z Pr(>F)
> Csize      1 7.1737 7.1737 0.99994 113923 4.7315  0.001 **
> Residuals  7 0.0004 0.0001 0.00006
> Total      8 7.1742
> ---
> Signif. codes:  0 ‘***’ 0.001 ‘**’ 0.01 ‘*’ 0.05 ‘.’ 0.1 ‘ ’ 1

> > On Sep 22, 2018, at 11:53 AM, Adams, Dean [EEOBS] <dca...@iastate.edu> wrote:

> > Most interesting Charles.  So for shape ~ Csize, a non-phylogenetic regression has a relatively low R2 for CSize, but for the same data it is nearly 1.0 when doing phylogenetic regression. I have not seen a dataset quite that extreme in its difference before.
> >
> > This, to me leads to two more options. One is that there is something odd with your tree, and the other is that both size and shape are extremely highly correlated with your tree, leading to the high association in the PGLS. The latter can be investigated by evaluating the phylogenetic signal in size, and in shape. The former, by investigating the tree.

> > Of course you are absolutely right regarding the comparison. Here is the table for the same mean shapes and mean sizes with OLS as in procD.lm:

> > CS         1 0.0051021 0.0051021 0.21885 3.0064  1.52237  0.030 *

> > To get the mean shapes for species that appear on a tree I wrote a small function:
> > function(x,y){
> >   myList = list()
> >   for (i in 1:length(y$tip.label)){

> > For the mean sizes I just did: CS_means = tapply(CS, names(CS), mean) . Again, ensuring the names were all the same species name for each individual.

> > >

> > > Two: something in your procedures of obtaining average shapes, average sizes, or both is incorrect, causing a spurious and very high R2.

messages.subject: RE: [geomorph-r-package] Correction for multiple pairwise comparisons
messages.body_plain:
Daniel,

They are not.

Deciding whether to adjust for multiple comparisons, which correction procedure to use, and for which pairwise comparisons, are all user-based decisions. As such, geomorph does not force this on the user, and it must be done post-hoc.

What that means is that the user compares the observed pairwise significance values obtained from geomorph to some adjusted critical value (i.e., one adjusts the typical 0.05 cut-off to be some other value based on the number of tests and the correction procedure desired).

You can do it w just rgl and base functions....

# data
ply <- [read in your ply]

lm.nums <- 1:nrow(lms)

# alpha level sets transparency
plot3d(ply, col = adjustcolor("lightgrey", .3), alpha = .3, specular = 1,

text3d(lms, texts = lm.noms, adj=1)

Christy emailed her files to me directly. We're not sure what happened on her first try, but the code works. I've attached the R script, and I've pasted the images below, followed by a couple of instructions for the script.

messages.subject: Re: [geomorph-r-package] Re: State-dependent diversification
messages.body_plain:
It is possible to examine the relationship between phenotypic divergence and diversification rates, but not by the methods that you mentioned in your question (the methods for testing hypotheses about "state"-dependent diversification). Those methods relate discrete states to rates of diversification.  For examples of studies analyzing rates of phenotypic divergence to rates of diversification, see Rabosky, D. L. and D. C. Adams. 2012. Rates of morphological evolution are correlated with species richness in salamanders. Evolution 66:1807-1818 and  Zelditch, M. L., J. Li, L. A. P. Tran, and D. L. Swiderski. 2015. Relationships of diversity, disparity and their evolutionary rates in squirrels (Sciuridae). Evolution 69:1284–1300. Now, in our analysis of squirrels, we used methods that are among those criticized by Adams and Collyer (2018) but the model that is implemented for shape (Brownian Motion) gave grossly inaccurate estimates of disparity: simulating the data using the parameters of that model, the predicted disparity was twice the  observed value, rather than the 2-5% too high/low (that we obtained by simulating the data under the models we used for estimating "rates").  If you do plan to use likelihood-based methods (mvMORPH), I'd recommend using parametric bootstrapping when selecting a model, and assessing the model-misspecification rates, which can be distressingly high.  The more serious problem for relating rates of phenotypic divergence to rates of diversification is that evolutionary"rates" are model-dependent so if different clades evolve by different modes, their rates are incommensurate.

messages.body_plain:
Hi Mohamed,

Good question!  The Q value gpagen returns is related to the tol value that the Morpho package allows one to vary.  Q is the statistic calculated after every iteration to compare to tol (which yes, is arbitrary) to determine if additional GPA permutations should be run.  Increasing the number of sliding landmarks will indeed affect the convergence (by making it more difficult unless the tol value is made larger).  We could possibly add this argument to gpagen, but we have taken a different approach with the max.iter.  The issue is if the tol value is too small and Q does not approach it, GPA iterations will run ad infinitum.  Therefore, we allow the user to specify when to stop GPA and by viewing Q, one can decide if they are happy with the convergence or whether to increase max.iter and try again.  There is a point where changing tol or max.iter does not improve the solution; i.e., Q might have a basement level it cannot pass through more permutations.

We made this choice because whether semi-landmarks are on curves or surfaces, and whether one uses bending energy or minimized Procrustes distance, the tol value, as a choice, is unintuitive and variable but the maximum number of iterations is clear, will not cause infinite loops, and is just more user-controlled.  We could hypothetically add both arguments but we worried initially that someone accidentally making the tol value too large would have a GPA that results in inferior convergence, as that argument would override the max.iter choice.  (We chose the safer route.)

I could be swayed to reconsider if users really want to be able to change the tol value, though.

Cheers!
Mike

I am performing a trajectory.analysis on data containing two species at four ontogenetic stages. Here is the code I am using:

TA<-trajectory.analysis(shape~species*ds, iter=999, data=HPF)
summary(TA)
TA$aov.table
plot(TA, group.cols=c("magenta", "blue"))

Here is the resulting plot:

The centroids of each group seem to be offset toward the negative end of the first PC. Does anyone have any idea why the data is plotting this way and how I can correct it?

Thanks,

Karen

messages.body_plain:
I see.  Here are some possible explanations:

It is possible that this results from PCA performed on the fitted values rather than the observed values.  When performing PCA in SAS, did you simply perform PCA on the data or did you use the fitted values to generate a covariance matrix before projection of the original data?
It could be projection distortion because of huge shape difference between species.  The offsetting seems largest in the most distal group of Trog.  This seems less likely though.
It could be a functional error that is only now being revealed with your extreme example.  I have looked at the code and I do not think this is a direct problem, but I see how it could look like one, which brings me to the next one
Data imbalance.  The PCA is performed on the trajectory points (fitted values, yes, but not weighted fitted values).  Although there has to be balance among trajectory points, your example shows that you have more Homo specimens than Trog specimens, correct?  Therefore, the center of gravity for trajectory points can be shifted away from the center of gravity for the entire sample.

I think the fourth case is most likely and would not have been revealed earlier if most people tend to have close to balanced data.  If you were to perform PCA first and then take the means (centroids) of PC scores, this would not happen.

I am going to see if I can update the code and ask you to try your analysis again, after I update it (by installing from Github).  If it works, then I will be more convinced that accounting for imbalance is important.

I’ll have the updates done in a couple of hours.

Mike

messages.body_plain:
David,

The “means” are the trajectory points, define both by groups and sequence factors.  While our statement from the 2013 Hystix paper is not incorrect, taken in its most literal form - as the function currently does - weighting is ignored.  For example, the fitted values from a factorial ANOVA are the means for the different factor combinations; i.e., the trajectory points.  In a matrix of fitted values, some means will be represented more if one group is over-represented compared to another.  The pooled-covariance should be a weighted average, perhaps; i.e., the covariance matrix should be calculated from all fitted values rather than just the means.  For balanced data, this produces the same covariance matrices.

Mike

Karen,

What you did seems to be the same thing the trajectory,analysis function does except that you were centering the combined matrix (the trajectory.analysis centers each separately).  What looks appropriate though is probably a partial solution, as each centroid has equal weight.  So, you pulled residuals (observations - mean of observations plus group means) toward the group means.  The observations and their means will line up better, but you do not stay honest to the center of gravity of the scatter in the plot being the same as center of gravity of the data sample.

I suspect that generating a covariance matrix from the fitted values of the model, shape ~ species * ds, which will be different than the covariance matrix of means if one species is over-represented, will appropriate shift the means to align with the mean-centered data, as both would have the same overall mean.  Stated another way, the mean of your centroids is not the same as the mean of your data if the data are imbalanced, but the mean of the fitted values (which has means equal in number to group sizes) is the same.

For balanced data these considerations are not needed.  For nearly balanced data, imperfections are probably unnoticeable.  For substantially imbalanced data, apparently, we have learned projections will not be accurate.

Please be aware that not of this discussion impacts the trajectory analysis, just its visualization.

Mike

Dear Everyone,

As a conclusion to the issue discussed in this thread, let me report here the important points.

1. This was a plotting issue, not an analytical one.  Trajectory analysis involves finding the LS means for groups and sequential points in many permutations to define trajectories.  This was not in dispute.
2. Visualizing trajectories means projecting these means onto principal components.  Before projection, the means must be “centered” so that the overall mean is 0,0,0,… and covariance matrices calculated from these values are appropriate.
3. Centering by the mean of the LS means - the default when calling prcomp in R scripts - only works if sample size is the same for each group.
4. If group sizes are different, then means need to be centered by the overall mean of fitted values, which equals the overall mean of the data, rather than the mean calculated from the input values in prcomp.

We performed 3, not 4, in geomorph, but trajectory.analysis has been updated on Github to use appropriately weighted LS means.  You can install the update with,

devtools::install_github(“geomorphR/geomorph”, ref = “Stable”)

For those of you who have deeper R skills, you might be aware that the prcomp function has a “center” argument.  Leaving this NULL means the function calculates the mean from the data input.  That was the projection problem we had (did not center the LS means by the correct center of gravity), which goes undetected if data are balanced, like in our trajectory,analysis examples.

Many thanks to Karen for bringing this to our attention and helping to beta-test the updates!

Cheers!
Mike
